questions.enonce_markdown:
Construct Truth Tables for the following statements:

(i) $(M \cdot N) \vee (\sim M \supset N)$ (2 marks)

(ii) $(A \vee B) \cdot \sim A$ (2 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
With two statement letters there are $2^2 = 4$ rows. Each column is built from the columns before it.

**(i)** $(M \cdot N) \vee (\sim M \supset N)$

| $M$ | $N$ | $M \cdot N$ | $\sim M$ | $\sim M \supset N$ | $(M \cdot N) \vee (\sim M \supset N)$ |
|:-:|:-:|:-:|:-:|:-:|:-:|
| T | T | T | F | T | T |
| T | F | F | F | T | T |
| F | T | F | T | T | T |
| F | F | F | T | F | F |

The final column is T, T, T, F: the statement is **contingent** (false only when $M$ and $N$ are both false).

**(ii)** $(A \vee B) \cdot \sim A$

| $A$ | $B$ | $A \vee B$ | $\sim A$ | $(A \vee B) \cdot \sim A$ |
|:-:|:-:|:-:|:-:|:-:|
| T | T | T | F | F |
| T | F | T | F | F |
| F | T | T | T | T |
| F | F | F | T | F |

The final column is F, F, T, F: the statement is **contingent** (true only when $A$ is false and $B$ is true). Note that it is logically equivalent to $\sim A \cdot B$.

questions.enonce_markdown:
**ALTERNATIVE FOR THE VISUALLY IMPAIRED CANDIDATES ONLY**

(a) (i) What is the determining factor for validity of an argument on the truth table?

(ii) On what grounds can one pronounce a statement as a tautology based on the truth table? (2 x 2 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
**(i) The determining factor for validity.**

An argument is valid if and only if there is **no row of the truth table in which all the premises are true and the conclusion is false**. Such a row (a *counter-example*) is the only thing that matters: if it exists, the argument is invalid; if the premises are never all true together with a false conclusion, it is valid. (The truth value of the premises or of the conclusion taken alone is irrelevant: a valid argument may have false premises.)

**(ii) Grounds for pronouncing a statement a tautology.**

A statement (form) is a tautology when the **column under its main connective contains only T**: it comes out true in **every row**, that is, for every possible combination of truth values of its component statements. It is therefore true by virtue of its logical form alone, whatever the facts (example: $(P \cdot Q) \supset (P \vee Q)$).

questions.enonce_markdown:
Test the validity of the following arguments using the Truth Table Technique: (3 x 2 marks)

(i) $[P \cdot (Q \supset R)] \vee (\sim R \supset \sim Q)$

$R \vee (P \supset Q)$

$\therefore\ \sim Q \vee P$

(ii) $H \supset (G \vee I)$

$\therefore\ H \supset [H \cdot (G \vee I)]$
questions.corrige_markdown:
**Method.** List every assignment of truth values to the statement letters, compute each premise and the conclusion, and look for a row in which **all the premises are true and the conclusion is false**. If there is one the argument is **invalid** (that row is a counter-example); if there is none it is **valid**.

**(i)** Three letters, $2^3 = 8$ rows.

| $P$ | $Q$ | $R$ | $Q \supset R$ | $P \cdot (Q \supset R)$ | $\sim R \supset \sim Q$ | **Premise 1:** $[P \cdot (Q \supset R)] \vee (\sim R \supset \sim Q)$ | $P \supset Q$ | **Premise 2:** $R \vee (P \supset Q)$ | **Conclusion:** $\sim Q \vee P$ | Premises true, conclusion false? |
|:-:|:-:|:-:|:-:|:-:|:-:|:-:|:-:|:-:|:-:|:-:|
| T | T | T | T | T | T | T | T | T | T | no |
| T | T | F | F | F | F | F | T | T | T | no |
| T | F | T | T | T | T | T | F | T | T | no |
| T | F | F | T | T | T | T | F | F | T | no |
| F | T | T | T | F | T | T | T | T | F | **YES (counter-example)** |
| F | T | F | F | F | F | F | T | T | F | no |
| F | F | T | T | F | T | T | T | T | T | no |
| F | F | F | T | F | T | T | T | T | T | no |

In the row $P$ = F, $Q$ = T, $R$ = T both premises are true and the conclusion is false (F v F = F). The argument is **invalid**.

**(ii)** Three letters, 8 rows. The premise and the conclusion are compared.

| $H$ | $G$ | $I$ | $G \vee I$ | **Premise:** $H \supset (G \vee I)$ | $H \cdot (G \vee I)$ | **Conclusion:** $H \supset [H \cdot (G \vee I)]$ |
|:-:|:-:|:-:|:-:|:-:|:-:|:-:|
| T | T | T | T | T | T | T |
| T | T | F | T | T | T | T |
| T | F | T | T | T | T | T |
| T | F | F | F | F | F | F |
| F | T | T | T | T | F | T |
| F | T | F | T | T | F | T |
| F | F | T | T | T | F | T |
| F | F | F | F | T | F | T |

There is no row in which the premise is true and the conclusion false (the premise column and the conclusion column are identical). The argument is **valid**. (The conclusion is obtained from the premise by the rule of absorption, $p \supset q\ \therefore\ p \supset (p \cdot q)$.)

questions.enonce_markdown:
**ALTERNATIVE FOR THE VISUALLY IMPAIRED CANDIDATES ONLY**

(b) (i) What principle is operative in the short truth-table method for testing validity? Explain your answer.

(ii) How is the truth table applicable in computer systems? (3 x 2 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
**(i) The principle: reductio ad absurdum (indirect proof, proof by contradiction).**

The short truth-table method does not list all the rows. It **assumes the opposite of validity**, that is, it tries to give the **conclusion the value false and all the premises the value true**, and it follows what this forces on the statement letters.

- If the assignment is **impossible** (a letter would have to be both true and false), the supposition of invalidity is absurd, and the argument is **valid**.
- If a consistent assignment exists, it is a counter-example and the argument is **invalid**.

It rests on the definition of validity (no case of true premises with a false conclusion) and on the law of non-contradiction.

**(ii) Truth tables in computer systems.**

Truth tables define the **logic gates** (AND, OR, NOT, NAND, NOR, XOR) from which digital circuits and processors are built, using 1 for true and 0 for false. They are used to **design and simplify circuits** (Boolean algebra) and to **check that two circuits or expressions are equivalent**. In programming, the conditions of `if` and `while` instructions, and the connectives AND, OR, NOT, are evaluated according to truth tables; the same holds for Boolean searches in databases and search engines (e.g. "A AND NOT B").

questions.enonce_markdown:
Given that p and q are true statements and r and s are false statements, determine the Truth-Values of the following compound statements respectively: (2 x 3 marks)

(i) $\sim [P \vee (\sim r \cdot q)] \equiv (S \supset \sim P)$

(ii) $(r \cdot \sim q) \vee (p \supset q)$
questions.corrige_markdown:
Given: $p$ = T, $q$ = T, $r$ = F, $s$ = F. (In (i) the letters $P$ and $S$ are read as $p$ and $s$.) Work from the innermost parts outwards.

**(i)** $\sim [p \vee (\sim r \cdot q)] \equiv (s \supset \sim p)$

- Left side: $\sim r$ = T; $\sim r \cdot q$ = T $\cdot$ T = T; $p \vee (\sim r \cdot q)$ = T $\vee$ T = T; $\sim [\ldots]$ = **F**.
- Right side: $\sim p$ = F; $s \supset \sim p$ = F $\supset$ F = **T** (a false antecedent).
- Whole statement: F $\equiv$ T = **F**.

**Truth value of (i): False.**

**(ii)** $(r \cdot \sim q) \vee (p \supset q)$

- $\sim q$ = F; $r \cdot \sim q$ = F $\cdot$ F = F.
- $p \supset q$ = T $\supset$ T = T.
- Whole statement: F $\vee$ T = **T**.

**Truth value of (ii): True.**

questions.enonce_markdown:
**ALTERNATIVE FOR THE VISUALLY IMPAIRED CANDIDATES ONLY**

(c) Distinguish between the following pairs:

(i) A statement and statement form

(ii) A long and short truth table

(iii) Truth functional connective and logical constant (2 x 3 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
**(i) A statement and a statement form.**

A **statement** is a sentence that is definitely true or false (it has a truth value), for example *"Mary is a nurse"* or *"If John is a pilot then Mary is a nurse"*. A **statement form** is an expression that contains **statement variables** (letters such as $p$, $q$) instead of particular statements and has no truth value until the variables are replaced by statements; the statements obtained are its *substitution instances*. For example $p \supset q$ is a statement form, and *"If it rains, the road is wet"* is one of its instances. Validity belongs to argument forms, truth or falsity to statements.

**(ii) A long and a short truth table.**

A **long truth table** lists **all** the $2^n$ rows (for $n$ letters) and computes every column; it settles validity, tautology, contradiction and contingency but becomes heavy as letters increase. A **short truth table** works **indirectly** (by reductio ad absurdum): it supposes the conclusion false and the premises true and looks for **one** consistent row, or for a contradiction. It tests validity only, and does it much faster.

**(iii) A truth-functional connective and a logical constant.**

A **truth-functional connective** ($\sim$, $\cdot$, $\vee$, $\supset$, $\equiv$) joins statements so that the **truth value of the compound depends only on the truth values of the components**, as shown by its truth table. A **logical constant** is a symbol or word whose **meaning stays fixed** in every argument, as opposed to variables whose content changes (the truth-functional connectives, but also the quantifiers *all* and *some*, the copula, identity). Every truth-functional connective is a logical constant, but not every logical constant is a truth-functional connective (a quantifier is not).

questions.enonce_markdown:
Determine the rules of inference expressed by the following arguments respectively: (4 marks)

(i) $(L \cdot M) \supset (X \vee Y)$

$(X \vee Y) \supset (K \cdot N)$

$\therefore\ (L \cdot M) \supset (K \cdot N)$

(ii) $(B \vee A) \supset C$

$B \vee A$

$\therefore\ C$
questions.corrige_markdown:
**(i) Hypothetical Syllogism (HS), the pure hypothetical syllogism or chain argument.**

Both premises are conditionals; the **consequent of the first** ($X \vee Y$) is the **antecedent of the second**, and the conclusion is a conditional with the **antecedent of the first** ($L \cdot M$) and the **consequent of the second** ($K \cdot N$). Pattern: $p \supset q,\ q \supset r\ \therefore\ p \supset r$, with $p$ = $L \cdot M$, $q$ = $X \vee Y$, $r$ = $K \cdot N$. (Implication is transitive.)

**(ii) Modus Ponens (MP), the mode that affirms the antecedent.**

The first premise is a conditional whose antecedent is the compound $B \vee A$; the second premise **affirms that antecedent**; the conclusion affirms the consequent $C$. Pattern: $p \supset q,\ p\ \therefore\ q$, with $p$ = $B \vee A$ and $q$ = $C$.

(Both forms are valid; each can be checked by a truth table.)
themes: rules of inference and argument forms

questions.enonce_markdown:
**ALTERNATIVE FOR THE VISUALLY IMPAIRED CANDIDATES ONLY**

(d) Explain the principle operative in:

(i) The pure hypothetical syllogism.

(ii) The modus ponens argument. (4 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
**(i) The pure hypothetical syllogism: the transitivity of implication (the chain principle).**

If the first thing implies the second, and the second implies the third, then the first implies the third: $p \supset q,\ q \supset r\ \therefore\ p \supset r$. Both premises and the conclusion are conditionals; the **consequent of the first premise must be the antecedent of the second**, and the conclusion links the antecedent of the first to the consequent of the second. Example: *If it rains, the river rises; if the river rises, the bridge floods; therefore, if it rains, the bridge floods.* The principle is that of **transitivity**: the middle statement is a link that drops out of the conclusion.

**(ii) The modus ponens: affirming the antecedent.**

If a conditional statement is true and its **antecedent is true**, its **consequent must be true**: $p \supset q,\ p\ \therefore\ q$. The only way a conditional can be false is a true antecedent with a false consequent, and this is excluded, so when the antecedent is affirmed the consequent is affirmed ("the mode that affirms by affirming", *ponendo ponens*). The converse reasoning, from the consequent to the antecedent, is the fallacy of affirming the consequent.
themes: rules of inference and argument forms

questions.enonce_markdown:
Translate the following arguments into symbols: (3 marks)

(i) Some girls are mothers. All girls are females. Therefore some females are mothers.

(ii) Test the validity of the following argument using the Short Truth Table method. (2 marks)

$(P \cdot Q) \supset R$

$\sim (P \vee R)\ \ /\ \therefore\ \sim Q$
questions.corrige_markdown:
**(i) Symbolisation (predicate logic).**

Annotations: $Gx$: $x$ is a girl; $Mx$: $x$ is a mother; $Fx$: $x$ is a female.

- *Some girls are mothers:* $(\exists x)(Gx \cdot Mx)$
- *All girls are females:* $(x)(Gx \supset Fx)$
- *Therefore some females are mothers:* $(\exists x)(Fx \cdot Mx)$

$$(\exists x)(Gx \cdot Mx),\quad (x)(Gx \supset Fx)\quad \therefore\quad (\exists x)(Fx \cdot Mx)$$

(In categorical form it is the syllogism I A I in the third figure, **Disamis**, which is valid: some girl is a mother, and she is a female.)

**(ii) Short truth table.**

The short method tries to make the conclusion **false** and all the premises **true**; if that is possible the argument is **invalid**, if it leads to a contradiction it is **valid**.

1. Make the conclusion false: $\sim Q$ = F, so **$Q$ = T**.
2. Make premise 2 true: $\sim (P \vee R)$ = T, so $P \vee R$ = F, so **$P$ = F and $R$ = F**.
3. Check premise 1: $(P \cdot Q) \supset R$ = $($F $\cdot$ T$) \supset$ F = F $\supset$ F = **T**.

| $P$ | $Q$ | $R$ | $(P \cdot Q) \supset R$ | $\sim (P \vee R)$ | $\sim Q$ |
|:-:|:-:|:-:|:-:|:-:|:-:|
| F | T | F | T | T | F |

All the premises are true and the conclusion is false with $P$ = F, $Q$ = T, $R$ = F. No contradiction arises, so the argument is **invalid**.

questions.enonce_markdown:
**ALTERNATIVE FOR THE VISUALLY IMPAIRED CANDIDATES ONLY**

(e) (i) Explain why the A and E statements are do not have existential import in Boolean system. (3 marks)

(ii) What does it mean to say that a proposition has existential import? (2 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
**(ii) Existential import.**

A proposition has **existential import** when it **asserts (implies) that the class named by its subject term has members**, that is, that there are things of that kind. In the traditional (Aristotelian) logic all four standard propositions A, E, I, O are read as having existential import: "All $S$ are $P$" and "No $S$ are $P$" are taken to presuppose that $S$ exists, which is why the traditional square of opposition holds (subalternation, contraries and subcontraries).

**(i) Why A and E have none in the Boolean system.**

George Boole's interpretation (the modern one) treats classes as possibly **empty** and translates the propositions as statements about the emptiness or non-emptiness of classes:

- **A**: *All $S$ are $P$* means $S \cap \overline{P} = \varnothing$, "there is nothing that is $S$ and not $P$". If there are no $S$ at all, this is true (vacuously).
- **E**: *No $S$ are $P$* means $S \cap P = \varnothing$, "there is nothing that is both". It is also true when there are no $S$.
- **I** (*Some $S$ are $P$*) means $S \cap P \neq \varnothing$ and **O** (*Some $S$ are not $P$*) means $S \cap \overline{P} \neq \varnothing$: they alone **assert existence**.

Universal statements are often made about classes with no members ("All trespassers will be prosecuted", "All unicorns have one horn"), and they are not false because there are no trespassers or unicorns, so a universal proposition cannot be held to assert existence. Hence A and E say what must be absent, not what is present, and have **no existential import**; only I and O have it. The price is that, in the Boolean system, the traditional inferences that depend on existence (subalternation, contrariety, subcontrariety, conversion *per accidens*) are no longer valid.
